question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built in Python with a REST API and file-based logs. We started seeing inconsistent query results and occasional failures when multiple requests came in close together, so I took ownership of debugging it.

I first reproduced the issue by sending repeated API requests and comparing the returned data with the log entries. Then I traced the flow from the endpoint handler down to the storage layer and found that one part of the code was reading the data file while another part was writing to it without proper locking. That meant the system could return partially updated records or miss writes entirely. I also noticed our logs were too vague, so I added more structured log messages around request IDs, timestamps, and read/write operations to make the behavior easier to trace.

After that, I refactored the storage access so writes were atomic and added a simple lock around critical sections. I also updated the REST API responses to return clearer error messages when a request failed instead of just timing out. Once I made those changes, I reran the test cases and stress-tested the API with concurrent requests.

The result was that the inconsistent query bug stopped happening, and the failure rate during repeated requests dropped to zero in our tests. It also made future debugging much easier because we could follow each request through the logs end to end.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app that used Firebase for the backend. It was a course project, so the main goal was to build something functional and learn how the pieces fit together. The app let users sign in, view content, and interact with a simple interface, so it gave me a chance to work on both the front end and basic data handling.

My role was mostly assisting with the development. I helped build some of the React components, worked on connecting parts of the UI, and supported the Firebase setup for things like authentication and storing data. I also helped test the app and fix small issues as they came up.

It was a good experience because it helped me get more comfortable with React and understand how a real web app is structured. By the end, we had a working project that met the main requirements and gave me a better idea of how to work on a team and solve problems step by step.

One challenge I ran into was keeping the components organized as the app grew. At first, I had some repeated code, so I learned to break things into smaller reusable components. That made the project easier to manage and helped me understand React better.

Overall, the project was a good learning experience for me. It gave me more confidence working on a real front-end project, and I came away with a better understanding of how to build clean, user-friendly web applications.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I delivered a reporting feature under a pretty tight constraint: we needed to add a new analytics endpoint in Node.js without changing the existing API contract, because the frontend was already built against it and we didn’t have time for a redesign.

I personally owned the work end to end. The feature was to return a summary report with totals and breakdowns from existing data, and the main challenge was that the data model wasn’t ideal for reporting. Instead of adding a new service or doing a big refactor, I kept the change small and focused in the REST API layer and the query logic.

I started by checking the current routes and response shapes, then I wrote the new endpoint so it reused the existing controller structure. I added validation for the request filters, like date range and report type, so we wouldn’t return bad data or crash on missing fields. In the service layer, I built the aggregation logic to calculate the metrics the report needed, and I made sure the response stayed consistent with the rest of the API.

Because the deadline was tight, I used tests to keep the change safe. I added unit tests for the aggregation functions and API tests for the endpoint itself, covering valid requests, empty results, and invalid input. That helped me move quickly without breaking the existing routes. I also checked the response payload against the frontend expectations so the integration stayed smooth.

What I learned from that was how to keep a feature small and reliable when there isn’t room for a larger redesign. I had to make practical tradeoffs, like reusing existing code paths and focusing on the exact report the product needed, instead of trying to solve everything at once.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python backend REST API for managing student course data, and I personally owned the debugging when one of the endpoints started returning inconsistent results. The issue was with a `GET /courses/<id>` endpoint that sometimes returned a 500 error, but only for certain records, so it was hard to reproduce at first.

I started by checking the application logs and adding a few more debug statements around the request handler, the database query, and the response serialization. From the logs, I found that the failure happened when a course had a `null` value in an optional field, and my code was assuming that field was always a string. That caused an `AttributeError` during formatting.

I fixed it by updating the serializer to handle missing values safely and added validation in the API layer so the response always followed the same schema. I also wrote a couple of tests for the edge cases, including records with empty and missing fields.

After that, the endpoint stopped failing, and the error rate for that route dropped to zero in my local testing. It also made the API more reliable overall, and I learned a lot about using logs to trace issues instead of guessing where the bug was.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:

I used React and JavaScript, and I helped with building a few of the components and making the pages work together.

I wasn’t the main person driving the whole project, but I assisted with the front-end work and helped fix some issues when things weren’t displaying correctly. I also spent time making sure the app felt clean and easy to use. It was a good experience for me because I got to practice working with React in a real project setting and learn how to break a bigger idea into smaller parts.

Overall, the project came together pretty well, and it helped me get more comfortable with front-end development and working with a team.

question: Tell me about something you learned during your studies.
answer:
One thing I learned during my studies was how much my approach changes when I stop trying to do everything alone and actually talk things through with other people. In one of my coursework projects, we had to work on a group assignment, and at first I thought it would just be easier to handle my part quietly and keep moving. But after a while I realized that if we didn’t check in with each other, we ended up repeating work or missing small things.

It also taught me that I’m not always going to get things right the first time, and that’s okay. I got better at asking questions earlier instead of waiting until I was stuck. I think that was a useful lesson for me, because it made me more comfortable with being unsure and just learning as I go.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: I couldn’t change the existing database schema or break any of the current API responses because other parts of the app were already depending on them.

I personally owned the feature from implementation through testing. The goal was to add a summary report that grouped usage data by date and returned totals for things like active users, event counts, and top actions. Since I couldn’t introduce a new table or do a big refactor, I had to work within the existing data model and make the logic fit into the current service layer.

What I did was first map out the existing endpoints and data flow so I could reuse as much as possible. Then I added a new REST endpoint in Node.js that accepted query parameters like date range and report type. In the service layer, I wrote the aggregation logic to process the raw records in memory after fetching them from the existing repository methods. I also made sure the response format stayed consistent with the rest of the API, so it was easy for the frontend to consume.

Because the constraint meant I had to be careful about regressions, I added tests around the new endpoint and the service logic. I wrote unit tests for the aggregation functions, including edge cases like empty datasets, invalid date ranges, and records missing optional fields. I also added API tests to verify the status codes and response shape. That helped me catch a couple of issues early, like a date parsing bug and an off-by-one problem in the range filtering.

It was a good learning experience for me because I had to balance delivering the feature quickly with keeping the existing system stable. I think the main thing I learned was how to work within constraints by reusing what’s already there, keeping the change focused, and relying on tests to give me confidence before merging.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python backend REST API for managing student submissions, and I ran into a bug where some requests were failing with a 500 error only in certain cases. I personally owned the debugging because I was responsible for the API endpoint and the logs.

I started by reproducing the issue with Postman and then checked the application logs. The error wasn’t happening on every request, only when the payload had an empty optional field. In the logs, I saw a `KeyError` coming from a dictionary lookup in the request handler. The problem was that I was assuming the JSON body always contained that field, but in reality the client could omit it.

To fix it, I updated the endpoint to validate the request body before processing it. I added explicit checks for required fields, used `.get()` for optional values, and returned a clear `400 Bad Request` response with a helpful error message instead of letting the server crash. I also added a couple of tests for the missing-field cases so the same issue wouldn’t come back.

After the fix, the 500 errors for that endpoint dropped to zero in my test runs, and the API became much more reliable because invalid input was handled cleanly instead of breaking the request.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
In my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: the data model was still changing, but we needed something usable for demo and testing purposes quickly.

I personally owned the feature end to end. The requirement was to return a summary report for a date range, including totals and a few grouped metrics, but I couldn’t rely on the final database schema because some fields were still being finalized. So I designed the endpoint to be flexible and defensive. I added a REST route in Node.js that accepted the date filters, validated the input, and then built the response from the fields that were stable at that point. Where the data could vary, I used fallback logic so the API wouldn’t break if a record was missing an optional field.

I also made sure the feature was testable from the start. I wrote unit tests for the service layer to cover the aggregation logic, especially edge cases like empty results, invalid dates, and partial records. Then I added API tests to verify the endpoint returned the expected JSON structure and status codes. Because the schema was still evolving, I kept the tests focused on behavior rather than exact implementation details, which made them easier to maintain.

The main constraint was time, so I had to keep the implementation simple and avoid overengineering. Instead of building a more complex reporting engine, I used straightforward query and transformation logic in Node.js, and I documented the assumptions clearly so it would be easier to extend later. That helped me deliver a feature that was stable enough for the project stage we were in, while still leaving room to adapt once the data model was finalized.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python backend REST API for managing user submissions. I personally owned the debugging when one endpoint started failing intermittently in testing. The issue was that the API would return a 500 error only for certain payloads, but the error message wasn’t clear from the client side.

I started by checking the application logs and tracing the request flow through the route handler, service layer, and database call. I found that the failure happened when the request body was missing an optional field, and my code was assuming it always existed. That caused a `KeyError` before the validation step could run. I also noticed that the logs were too vague, so I added more structured logging around the request data and exception path to make the failure easier to trace.

I fixed it by changing the handler to use safe access with `.get()`, adding explicit validation for required fields, and returning a proper 400 response instead of letting it crash. After that, I reran the test cases and manually tested several payload variations. The endpoint stopped failing, and the error rate for that route went from a few failures per test run to zero in the final version.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built in Python with a REST API, and I was responsible for debugging a problem where some records were being saved correctly but not always returned correctly through the API. I personally owned the investigation because I had written most of the request-handling and logging code.

I started by reproducing the issue with a few test requests and then traced the flow from the API endpoint into the database layer. I used the logs to compare the request payload, the SQL queries being executed, and the response data. That helped me narrow it down to a mismatch between how I was serializing the stored data and how I was reading it back. In one case, the code was converting a field to a string before saving it, but the retrieval logic was still treating it like a nested object, so the API response was inconsistent.

I fixed that by standardizing the data format in the repository layer, adding stricter validation in the REST endpoint, and improving the log messages so each request had a clear request ID and step-by-step trace. After that, I reran the full test set and added a few regression tests for the failing cases.

The result was that the API became consistent for all tested records, and I reduced the number of failing test cases from 4 out of 12 to 0. It also made future debugging much easier because I could follow the logs end to end.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app for a course project. It was basically a small frontend app where users could move through different pages and interact with some simple features, and I helped build parts of the interface using React and JavaScript.

My role was more of an assisting role, so I wasn’t leading the whole project, but I did help with things like creating components, making the layout work, and fixing bugs when something wasn’t displaying correctly. I also worked with the rest of the team to make sure the pages felt consistent and the app was usable.

It was a good learning experience for me because I got more comfortable with React and how to break a project into smaller pieces. I also learned a lot from seeing how the team handled problems and put everything together. In the end, we finished the project and it worked well enough for the class, so I felt good about what we built.

question: Tell me about something you learned during your studies.
answer:
One thing I learned during my studies was how much easier a group project goes when everyone is clear about what they’re doing from the start. I was part of a coursework assignment where we had to work together on a presentation and report, and at first it felt a bit messy because people had different ideas and worked at different speeds. I didn’t do anything especially big, but I was involved in the group discussions and helped keep track of what we had already covered.

What stood out to me was that communication matters a lot more than I expected. Even simple things like checking in, asking questions early, and making sure everyone understood the plan made a difference. I also learned that it’s okay not to know everything straight away, because part of studying is figuring things out as you go and being willing to adjust. That experience made me more comfortable working with other people and more aware of how I approach tasks.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app I built as part of my course work. It was a simple portfolio-style application where users could view different sections, like an about page, projects, and contact information. I used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and React to put the app together.

My main responsibility was building the front-end components and making sure the layout was clean and easy to use. I worked on breaking the page into reusable parts, like the navigation bar, project cards, and footer. I also spent time on the styling so the app looked consistent and worked well on different screen sizes.

One challenge for me was getting comfortable with how React organizes a project, especially thinking in components instead of just writing everything in one page. At first, I had to spend extra time understanding how to structure things properly, but that helped me improve a lot.

By the end of the project, I had a working web app that looked polished and was easy to navigate. More importantly, I learned how to plan a small front-end project, build it step by step, and debug issues on my own. It was a really good learning experience for me and gave me more confidence working with React.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool, and I was responsible for delivering a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: we had to add the feature without breaking the existing REST API responses that the frontend already depended on, and I also had limited time to implement it because I was balancing it with other tasks.

The feature itself was to return summarized usage data for a selected date range, like total events, daily counts, and a breakdown by category. I owned the implementation end to end in Node.js, so I started by checking the existing API structure and the data shape the frontend was already using. I wanted to avoid changing the contract, so I added the new logic in a separate service layer instead of putting everything directly in the route handler. That made it easier to keep the endpoint clean and also easier to test.

The main technical challenge was making the query efficient enough while still keeping the code simple. I built the aggregation in Node.js so the API could calculate the summary from the raw records, and I made sure to validate the query parameters first, especially the start and end dates. I also handled edge cases like empty results and invalid ranges, because I knew those would be common in a reporting tool.

Since the constraint was not to introduce regressions, I wrote tests around the new endpoint and the helper functions. I covered the happy path, missing parameters, invalid date formats, and cases where there was no data for the requested range. I used those tests to confirm that the existing REST API behavior stayed the same and that the new response format matched what the frontend expected.

What I learned from that feature was how important it is to work within constraints without overcomplicating the solution. I had to be careful about API compatibility, keep the implementation modular, and rely on tests to give me confidence before merging.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built with Python and a REST API, and I was responsible for debugging a performance issue that was making the app feel unreliable. Users could create and query records through the API, but some requests were randomly timing out, especially when the dataset grew.

I owned the investigation end to end. I started by adding more detailed logging around the API endpoints, the database calls, and the request timings so I could see exactly where the slowdown was happening. From the logs, I noticed the slow requests were mostly tied to repeated full-table scans in one query path. The code was fetching more data than needed and then filtering it in Python instead of pushing the filtering into the database layer.

I fixed it by changing the query logic so the database handled the filtering directly, and I also cleaned up a couple of inefficient loops in the Python service. After that, I reran the same test cases and compared the logs before and after. The average response time for the affected endpoint dropped from around 1.8 seconds to under 300 milliseconds, and the timeouts stopped happening in our demo runs.

What I took from that was that good logging made the problem much easier to isolate, and even in a small project, small changes in where the work happens can make a big difference in performance.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: I couldn’t change the existing database schema, and I also had to keep the response fast enough for the UI to load without delays.

I personally owned the feature end to end. The goal was to add a summary report that grouped events by date and category, but the raw data was a bit messy and the API already had existing clients depending on the current response format. So I had to be careful not to break anything while still adding the new functionality.

I started by breaking the work into small pieces. First, I checked the existing routes and service layer to understand where the new endpoint fit best. Then I wrote the API contract and added tests before implementing the logic, so I had a clear target for the response shape. In the Node.js service, I used a query that pulled only the fields I needed instead of fetching full records, because I wanted to keep the payload smaller and avoid extra processing. I also handled grouping in the service layer rather than in the route handler, so the code stayed easier to test.

One constraint was that the data could include missing or inconsistent category values, so I added normalization logic to map empty values to a default label instead of letting the report break. I also made sure the endpoint returned predictable dates in ISO format, because the frontend was going to chart the results. For testing, I added unit tests for the grouping and normalization logic, plus integration tests for the REST endpoint to confirm the status codes and response structure.

The main thing I learned from that feature was how important it is to work within constraints without overcomplicating the solution. I had to keep the implementation simple, testable, and compatible with the existing API, and that made me more careful about how I structure backend features.

I also realised that I tend to be more comfortable once I understand the overall plan, so that was useful for me to notice about myself too. It wasn’t really about one big moment, more that the whole experience showed me how important communication and patience are when you’re working with other people.

question: Describe a project where you had to debug a difficult issue.
answer:
One project I worked on was a mobile app for a course project using React and Firebase. I was helping with the front-end and some of the data flow, and we ran into a bug where certain user actions were not saving correctly, but only sometimes. That made it hard to track down because it didn’t happen every time.

I helped by testing different steps in the app, checking the browser console, and comparing when the issue happened versus when it worked. We eventually found that the problem was related to how the app was handling the data before sending it to Firebase. I worked with the team to adjust that part and re-test it several times.

It was a good learning experience for me because it showed me how important it is to debug carefully and not assume the first thing you see is the real cause. In the end, we got the issue resolved and the app was working more reliably.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built in Python with a REST API, and I was responsible for debugging a performance issue that was causing slow responses and occasional timeouts.

I noticed from the logs that the API was spending most of its time repeatedly scanning the same records instead of using the indexes we had already built. I owned the investigation end to end: I reproduced the issue locally, added more detailed logging around the query path, and compared the request timings before and after each step. That helped me narrow it down to one endpoint that was doing a full table scan on every request because the filter logic was applied after fetching the data.

I fixed it by moving the filtering into the database query layer, adding an index on the most commonly queried field, and cleaning up the REST handler so it returned only the needed columns. I also added log messages for query duration and result count so we could catch similar issues faster in the future.

After the change, the average response time for that endpoint dropped from about 1.2 seconds to around 180 milliseconds in my tests, and the timeout errors stopped showing up in the logs. It was a good example of how I used logs and debugging to improve both the performance and maintainability of the system.

question: Describe a project where you had to choose between two technical approaches.
answer:
In one of my course projects, I worked on a full-stack student platform using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and I had to choose between two ways to build the student dashboard. One option was to make everything on a single page and update the content dynamically with JavaScript. The other was to split it into separate pages for things like profile, assignments, and announcements.

My main task was to help decide which approach would be easier to build and maintain for our team. At first, the single-page version seemed more modern, but I realized it would take more time for us to manage all the interactions and keep the code organized, especially since we were still learning. So I suggested we go with separate pages and keep the JavaScript focused on the parts that really needed interactivity.

That choice made the project simpler to finish on time, and it was easier for us to test and debug. I learned that the “best” technical solution is not always the most advanced one — it depends on the team’s experience, the timeline, and what the project actually needs.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I was responsible for adding a new reporting endpoint that had to be delivered within a pretty tight time constraint. The main challenge was that the existing data model was not fully optimized for the exact report the product needed, so I had to make sure I delivered something useful without taking the system apart.

I owned the feature end to end. First, I reviewed the existing API routes and the data we already had available, then I mapped out the report requirements into a response shape that could be returned efficiently. I decided to keep the implementation simple and reuse the current service layer instead of introducing a lot of new abstraction, because the deadline meant I needed a solution that was reliable and easy to test.

On the Node.js side, I added the endpoint, handled query parameters for filtering by date range, and made sure the response included the aggregated metrics the frontend needed. I also paid attention to validation and error handling, so if someone passed an invalid date or missing parameter, the API would return a clear 400 response instead of failing deeper in the code.

Because the constraint was time, I focused heavily on tests to reduce risk. I wrote unit tests for the aggregation logic and API tests for the route behavior, including success cases and edge cases like empty datasets and invalid input. That helped me catch a couple of issues early, like a date parsing mismatch and one case where the totals were being calculated incorrectly when there were no records.

I had to balance speed with quality, so I kept the implementation scoped to the required report rather than trying to generalize everything for future use. That let me deliver the feature within the constraint while still keeping the code readable and covered by tests.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built in Python with a REST API, and I was responsible for debugging a problem where requests were intermittently failing and some records were not being saved correctly.

I started by checking the logs and noticed that the failures were not random — they were happening after certain update and delete requests. I traced the issue through the API layer into the database logic and found that we had inconsistent handling of transaction commits and error cases. In a few paths, the code would return a success response before the write was fully completed, and in other cases exceptions were being swallowed, so the API looked healthy even when the database operation had failed.

I fixed this by tightening the request flow: I added clearer exception handling, made sure each write operation either completed fully or rolled back cleanly, and improved the logging so each request had a request ID and a more specific error message. I also added a few targeted tests for the endpoints that had been failing, especially around edge cases like duplicate inserts and invalid IDs.

After the changes, the failing requests stopped, and the error rate in our test runs dropped from around 15% to 0% for those endpoints. The logs also became much easier to use for debugging, because I could trace a request from the API call all the way to the database action. That project taught me how important it is to make backend systems observable and to be very deliberate about error handling.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app I built as part of a course project. It was basically a small portfolio-style app where users could browse different pages and interact with some simple features. I used React and JavaScript for it, and I helped with things like building components, setting up the page structure, and making sure the app felt consistent across the different screens.

I mostly assisted with the front-end side of things, so I worked on reusable components and helped fix a few bugs when things weren’t displaying correctly. It was a good learning experience for me because I got more comfortable with React and how to break a project into smaller pieces. I also learned a bit about working through issues step by step instead of trying to solve everything at once.

Overall, it was a pretty useful project for me because it gave me hands-on experience with building something from scratch, and I felt like I came away with a better understanding of how a real web app comes together.

question: Describe a project where you had to choose between two technical approaches.
answer:
One project that comes to mind was a student platform I worked on as part of a course project. It was a full-stack style project, but my main work was on the front end using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

We had to decide between building the page interactions with plain JavaScript or using a more structured approach with reusable components. At first, the simpler option seemed faster, and since we were working under time pressure, that was tempting. But I was responsible for making sure the student dashboard and form interactions stayed easy to update, so I looked at how the pages might grow if we added more features later.

In the end, we chose the more structured approach because it would be easier to maintain and less confusing for the team. My part was to build the student-facing pages and make sure the navigation, form validation, and content updates worked smoothly. I also helped keep the layout consistent across the different pages.

What I learned from that project was that the fastest option is not always the best one. Even in a small project, it helps to think about maintainability and how other people will work with the code later. That experience made me more careful about weighing short-term speed against long-term clarity.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: the data model was still changing, but we needed something usable for the demo and the early users.

I personally owned the feature end to end. The requirement was to return a summary report for a selected date range, grouped by event type, with totals and basic trend data. The constraint was that I couldn’t rely on a fully stable schema yet, so I had to design the endpoint in a way that would be easy to adapt without rewriting everything later.

I started by defining the API contract first, so the frontend and I had a clear shape to work with. I added a GET endpoint that accepted query parameters like `startDate`, `endDate`, and `groupBy`. In the service layer, I kept the logic separated from the route handler so the controller stayed thin. That made it easier to test and also easier to change the aggregation logic later if the data structure changed.

Because the data was still evolving, I wrote the aggregation code defensively. I validated the incoming query params, handled missing or invalid dates, and made sure the response always returned a consistent format, even when there was no data. I also used a small mapping layer between the raw records and the response object, so if fields changed in the database or API payload, I wouldn’t have to touch the route contract.

Testing was a big part of the work. I added unit tests for the service logic to cover the main cases: valid date ranges, empty results, invalid input, and grouping by different event types. I also added API tests for the endpoint itself to verify the status codes and response shape. Since the project was in Node.js, I used the test suite to catch a couple of edge cases early, like date parsing issues and off-by-one problems with the range filter.

The main thing I learned was how to keep the feature simple but flexible when the requirements aren’t fully stable. I had to make a few trade-offs, but by keeping the controller, service, and mapping logic separate, I was able to deliver the feature in a way that was easy to maintain and test.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
Sure — on my portfolio project, I had to deliver a reporting feature under a pretty tight constraint because the API contract for the analytics data was still changing while I was building the frontend and backend pieces.

I personally owned the work for the feature delivery, so I started by breaking the problem into smaller parts. The feature was a reporting endpoint in a Node.js app that needed to return summary analytics for a date range, grouped by things like event type and day. The constraint was that I couldn’t rely on the final response shape being stable, and I also had a limited amount of time to get something working end-to-end.

To handle that, I designed the REST API in a way that was flexible but still predictable. I kept the route simple, like a `GET /reports/summary` endpoint, and I made sure the query parameters were explicit, such as `startDate`, `endDate`, and `groupBy`. In the service layer, I separated the data transformation logic from the controller so I could adjust the aggregation rules without rewriting the route handler. That helped because when the response format changed slightly, I only had to update the mapping logic in one place.

I also leaned heavily on tests. I wrote unit tests for the aggregation functions and controller tests for the endpoint behavior, especially around edge cases like missing dates, empty results, and invalid query parameters. Since the API was still moving, the tests acted like a safety net and helped me refactor quickly without breaking the existing behavior. I used the tests to lock in the expected contract as I understood it at the time, which made it easier to keep moving even with uncertainty.

One specific thing I did was add a fallback structure in the response so the frontend could still render the report even if some metrics were unavailable. For example, if a grouping returned no rows, I returned an empty array instead of `null`, and I made sure the totals defaulted to zero. That reduced the amount of special-case handling needed on the client side.

Overall, the main challenge was delivering something usable while the inputs were still shifting. I handled that by keeping the Node.js code modular, keeping the REST API contract clear, and using tests to protect the feature as I iterated.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app I built as part of a course project. It was a simple front-end application where users could browse content, interact with different sections, and navigate between pages smoothly.

My main task was to build the user interface and make sure the app was organized and easy to use. I worked with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and React to create the layout, style the pages, and handle basic user interactions. I also spent time making sure the components were reusable and that the app felt consistent across the different screens.

One challenge for me was keeping everything structured as the project grew. At first, I had some messy code and repeated parts, so I learned how important it is to break the UI into smaller components and plan the structure before building too much. That helped me understand React better and made the project easier to maintain.

Overall, it was a good learning experience because I got more comfortable working with front-end tools and building something from start to finish. It also helped me improve my problem-solving and gave me a better understanding of how to turn an idea into a working web app.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a feature under a pretty tight constraint: I needed to add a new reporting endpoint without breaking the existing API contract, and I also had limited time to implement it because I was balancing it with other tasks.

The feature I owned was a summary report endpoint that returned aggregated usage data for a date range. The main challenge was that the data model wasn’t designed for reporting at first, so I had to work within the existing structure instead of doing a bigger refactor. I started by checking the current routes, controllers, and service layer to see where I could add the logic cleanly. Then I designed the endpoint so it would accept query parameters like `startDate`, `endDate`, and `groupBy`, and I made sure to validate those inputs before running any database queries.

Because of the time constraint, I focused on keeping the implementation simple and reliable. I wrote the aggregation logic in the service layer so the controller stayed thin, and I reused existing repository methods where possible instead of introducing a lot of new code. I also added tests for the main cases: valid date ranges, missing parameters, and edge cases like empty results. I used those tests to catch a couple of issues early, like inconsistent date formatting and a case where the endpoint was returning the wrong status code for invalid input.

I also had to be careful with performance, since the report could be called with a larger date range. So I made sure the query only selected the fields needed for the report and avoided extra processing in Node.js when the database could handle the aggregation. I documented the endpoint in the README and kept the response shape consistent with the rest of the API so it would be easy to use.

What I learned from that was how to deliver something useful without overengineering it. I had to make trade-offs, stay close to the existing codebase, and use tests to keep the feature safe while moving quickly.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In one of my course projects, I worked on a small database system built with Python and a REST API. We started seeing inconsistent data and occasional failed requests, so I took ownership of debugging it.

I began by tracing the issue through the API logs and database logs to find where the requests were breaking. I noticed that some endpoints were writing partial records when validation failed, and in a few cases the error handling was swallowing exceptions, which made the system look like it had succeeded when it hadn’t. I reproduced the problem locally with specific test requests, then added more detailed logging around the request payload, validation step, and database write operation so I could see exactly where the flow was failing.

After that, I fixed the validation logic to reject bad input before any database write happened, and I updated the API responses so failures returned clear status codes and messages. I also cleaned up the logging so errors were consistent and easier to trace.

As a result, the number of failed or inconsistent writes dropped to zero in our test runs, and debugging became much faster because we could identify the exact failure point from the logs instead of guessing. That project taught me how important it is to make systems observable and to fix the root cause, not just the symptom.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: I needed to add the feature without breaking the existing API contract, and I also had limited time to make changes because I was working around the rest of the project schedule.

The feature was a summary report endpoint that returned aggregated usage data for a date range. I personally owned the implementation end to end. I started by checking the existing routes, controllers, and service layer so I could fit the new endpoint into the current structure instead of creating something separate. I also reviewed the existing tests first, because I wanted to make sure I understood what behavior was already covered before I changed anything.

The main constraint was that the data model wasn’t ideal for reporting, so I couldn’t just query one field and return the result. I had to combine data from multiple records, group it by day, and calculate totals and averages in the service layer. To keep it manageable, I broke the work into small steps: first I built the basic endpoint, then I added the aggregation logic, and then I wrote tests for the edge cases like empty results, invalid date ranges, and partial data.

I used Jest to add unit tests for the service functions and API tests for the route itself. That helped me catch a couple of issues early, like handling timezone boundaries incorrectly and returning the wrong status code when the query parameters were missing. I fixed those before merging.

So overall, I delivered the feature by keeping the implementation simple, fitting it into the existing Node.js REST structure, and leaning on tests to make sure the new reporting behavior was stable even with the time and data constraints.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python backend REST API for managing student assignments, and I ran into a bug where some requests were failing with a 500 error only in certain cases. I personally owned the debugging because I had written the endpoint and the service logic.

The issue was that the API worked fine for normal inputs, but when a user submitted an empty or partially missing payload, the server would crash instead of returning a clean validation error. I started by checking the logs and tracing the request flow from the route handler to the service layer. The logs showed that the failure happened when the code tried to access a nested field that didn’t exist, so it was raising a `KeyError` before any validation happened.

To fix it, I added explicit request validation at the API layer, used `.get()` for optional fields, and moved the required-field checks before any database or business logic. I also added more detailed logging around the request body and validation failures so future issues would be easier to trace. After that, I tested the endpoint with valid payloads, empty JSON, missing fields, and wrong data types.

The result was that the endpoint stopped crashing and returned proper 400 responses instead of 500s. In testing, I reduced the failing cases from about 3 common input scenarios to 0, and the API became much more stable and easier to debug.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool, and I was asked to add a new reporting endpoint that would return summary metrics for a date range. The main constraint was that I had to deliver it without changing the existing API contract for the front end, and I also had to keep it within the time I had available because I was balancing it with other tasks.

I owned the feature end to end. I started by checking the existing Node.js REST API structure and the current data flow, then I mapped out what the endpoint needed to return so I wouldn’t break anything already using the service. I kept the implementation simple: I added a new route, built the controller logic to validate query parameters like startDate and endDate, and then wrote the service layer to aggregate the data into totals and averages before sending the response.

Because the constraint was mostly around stability and time, I focused on making the changes low-risk. I reused the existing patterns in the codebase instead of introducing a new abstraction, and I added tests around the new endpoint to cover valid requests, missing parameters, and edge cases like an empty result set. I also wrote a couple of integration-style tests to make sure the response shape matched what the front end expected.

What I learned from that was how important it is to work within the existing system instead of trying to over-engineer a solution. Even as a junior developer, I was able to break the problem into small pieces, implement it carefully in Node.js, and verify it with tests so the feature could be added without disrupting the rest of the API.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built in Python with a REST API, and I was responsible for debugging a performance issue that was causing slow responses and occasional failed requests.

I started by checking the logs and noticed that a few endpoints were repeatedly hitting the database with the same queries inside loops. I traced the issue through the API layer and found that one route was making multiple separate calls to fetch related records instead of doing one joined query. I also saw that some errors were being swallowed, so it was hard to tell when a query was failing versus just taking too long.

I fixed it by refactoring the endpoint to reduce duplicate database calls, adding better error logging with request IDs, and making the log messages more specific so I could see exactly which query and payload caused a problem. I also added a simple timing log around the slowest operations so we could compare performance before and after the change.

question: Describe a project where you had to choose between two technical approaches.
answer:
In one of my course projects, I worked on a full-stack student platform using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. My main task was to help build the student dashboard, where users could view their assignments, deadlines, and basic profile information.

We had to choose between two approaches for displaying the data. One option was to load everything at once when the page opened, which would have been simpler to build. The other option was to load the information in smaller parts as the user needed it, which would take a bit more work but would make the page feel faster and cleaner.

I helped compare both options by thinking about the user experience and how much time we had for the project. Since this was a student platform and the dashboard could grow over time, we decided to go with the second approach. That meant we could keep the page organized and avoid overwhelming the user with too much information at once.

My part was mainly implementing the front-end side of that decision and making sure the layout still felt simple and easy to use. It was a good learning experience for me because I saw how technical choices affect both the user and the development process. I also learned that sometimes the best option is not the easiest one to build, but the one that works better in the long run.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API. The feature I delivered under a constraint was a reporting endpoint that returned summary metrics for a given date range, but I had a tight deadline and I also had to make sure the response stayed fast because the frontend needed it for a dashboard.

I personally owned the feature from the API design through implementation and testing. The main constraint was that the data source was not ideal for heavy queries, so I couldn’t just do a lot of work on every request. I started by breaking the problem down into the exact fields the dashboard needed, like total events, unique users, and daily counts. That helped me avoid overengineering it.

I implemented the endpoint in Node.js using Express, and I kept the logic separated into a controller, service, and data-access layer so it was easier to test. In the service layer, I added validation for the query parameters, especially the start and end dates, because I wanted to fail fast on bad input. Then I wrote the aggregation logic to group records by day and calculate the summary values the frontend expected.

Because of the time constraint, I focused on the most important test coverage first. I wrote unit tests for the service logic and API tests for the endpoint using a test framework, including cases for valid ranges, missing parameters, and invalid dates. I also tested edge cases like an empty result set so the response would still be predictable.

I had to make a few tradeoffs to keep it deliverable. For example, instead of building a more complex caching layer or background job, I kept the implementation simple and optimized the query shape as much as I could within the project scope. I also made sure the JSON response was consistent and easy for the frontend to consume, which reduced back-and-forth during integration.

So overall, I delivered a working reporting feature under a tight deadline by keeping the scope focused, writing the core logic cleanly in Node.js, and making sure it was covered with tests.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python backend REST API for managing student course data, and I ran into a bug where one endpoint was randomly returning 500 errors in production-like testing. I personally owned the debugging for it.

The issue was happening on a `POST /enrollments` endpoint. Locally it worked most of the time, but in the test environment it would fail when the request payload included an optional `notes` field. I started by checking the API logs and tracing the request through the service layer and database call. The logs showed the failure was coming from a `TypeError` during JSON serialization, because I was passing a Python `datetime` object and a `None` value into a response object that the framework couldn’t serialize cleanly.

I reproduced it with the exact payload from the logs, then added more structured logging around the request body, validation step, and response creation. That helped me confirm the bug was not in the database query itself, but in how I was building the response after the insert. I fixed it by normalizing the response data before returning it: converting the datetime to ISO 8601 format, filtering out null fields, and adding a validation check so the endpoint rejected malformed input earlier with a 400 instead of failing later with a 500.

After the fix, I reran the full API test suite and manually tested the endpoint with several payload variations. The 500 errors stopped completely, and the endpoint became stable across all test cases. I also documented the logging pattern I used so it would be easier to debug similar issues later.

question: Describe a project where you had to choose between two technical approaches.
answer:
One project that comes to mind was a full-stack student platform I worked on for a course project. I was responsible for building part of the front end using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and we had to decide how to handle the student dashboard.

We had two options: either build everything as one simple page that showed all the information at once, or split it into separate sections and load content as the user clicked through. At first, the one-page approach seemed easier because it would be faster to build, and since it was a student project, we wanted to keep things manageable.

My task was to work on the dashboard layout and make sure it was easy to use. After thinking it through, I suggested the second approach because the dashboard had a lot of different information, like assignments, announcements, and profile details. Putting everything on one page would have made it feel crowded and harder to navigate.

We chose to organize it into sections instead. I helped build the navigation and the different content areas, and that made the interface much cleaner. It also helped us keep the code more organized, which was useful when we needed to make changes later.

What I learned from that project was that the simplest technical option is not always the best one for the user. Even on a smaller project, it’s important to think about usability and maintainability, not just how quickly something can be built.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
In my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and a REST API, and I had to deliver a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: the data model was still changing while I was implementing it, but I still needed to get something stable enough for the frontend to use.

I personally owned the feature end to end. The goal was to add an endpoint that returned summary metrics for a selected date range, like total events, unique users, and a breakdown by category. The constraint was that I couldn’t rely on the database schema being finalized, so I had to design the API in a way that was flexible and wouldn’t break if a field changed slightly.

What I did was start by defining the response shape first, so I could agree on the contract before writing much code. I used Express for the route, and I kept the controller thin by moving the aggregation logic into a service layer. That made it easier to test and also easier to adjust if the underlying query changed. I wrote tests with Jest and Supertest for the main cases: valid date range, missing query parameters, empty results, and invalid dates. I also added a few unit tests around the aggregation logic so I could verify the calculations independently of the API layer.

Because of the constraint, I avoided overengineering the query. Instead of trying to build one very complex database call, I fetched the raw records and did some of the grouping in Node.js. That was simpler to adapt while the schema was still moving, and it let me keep the endpoint working while the rest of the project was still settling. I also made sure the response included clear defaults, like returning zero counts instead of null, so the frontend wouldn’t have to handle a lot of edge cases.

It was a good learning experience for me because I had to balance speed, test coverage, and flexibility. I learned that when requirements are still shifting, it helps to lock down the API contract early, keep the code modular, and write tests around the behavior rather than the exact implementation.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system built with Python and a REST API, and I was responsible for debugging a performance issue that was causing slow responses and occasional timeouts.

I started by checking the application logs and tracing the requests end to end. I noticed that one endpoint was making repeated database calls inside a loop, so a single request was triggering far more queries than it should have. I reproduced the issue locally, added a few more log statements around the API handler, and confirmed that the same records were being fetched multiple times instead of being cached or retrieved in one query.

I fixed it by refactoring the endpoint to batch the database access and reuse the result set instead of querying repeatedly. I also cleaned up the error handling so the logs were more useful, and I added clearer log messages with request IDs so we could trace failures faster in the future.

After the change, the endpoint response time dropped from around 1.8 seconds to under 300 milliseconds in my tests, and the number of database calls per request went from about 20+ down to 2 or 3. It also made the logs much easier to debug, which helped the rest of the team verify the fix quickly.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
One feature I delivered under a constraint was an analytics reporting endpoint for a portfolio project I worked on. The main limitation was time: I had to add the feature without slowing down the rest of the API work, and I also needed to make sure the reporting data was accurate enough to be useful.

I personally owned the implementation of the endpoint in Node.js. The feature needed to return summary metrics from existing event data, like counts by date and basic totals over a selected time range. I started by checking the current data shape and the existing REST API patterns in the project so I could keep the new endpoint consistent. Then I designed the route to accept query parameters for things like start date, end date, and report type, and I made sure to validate those inputs before running any logic.

Because of the time constraint, I kept the implementation focused and avoided overengineering. I wrote the aggregation logic directly in the service layer instead of introducing extra abstraction that would have taken longer to build and test. I also paid attention to performance by reducing repeated data processing and making sure the response only included the fields the frontend needed.

Testing was important for me on this feature because the reporting logic had a few edge cases. I added unit tests for the date filtering and aggregation functions, and I wrote API tests to verify the endpoint returned the expected status codes and response structure for valid and invalid requests. I also tested cases like empty date ranges and missing query parameters, since those were likely to cause issues.

What I learned from that feature was how to balance delivery speed with code quality. I had to make practical decisions about scope, keep the API clean, and still make sure the tests covered the important behavior.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python REST API for managing student course data, and I ran into a bug where one endpoint was returning a 500 error only for certain requests. I personally owned the debugging because I was responsible for the backend route and the related service logic.

I started by checking the API logs and comparing successful and failing requests. I noticed the error happened when the request body was missing an optional field, but my code was still trying to access it directly like a required key. That caused a `KeyError` before the validation step could handle it. I traced it through the route handler, then updated the logic to use safer parsing and added explicit validation with clear error responses instead of letting the server crash.

After fixing that, I also added more structured logging around the request payload and validation path so it would be easier to debug similar issues later. I tested the endpoint with multiple cases: valid input, missing optional fields, and invalid data types. The result was that the 500 error was eliminated, and the endpoint consistently returned the correct 400-level response for bad input. It also reduced the time I spent debugging similar issues later because the logs were much clearer.

question: Describe a project where you had to choose between two technical approaches.
answer:
In one of my course projects, I worked on a full-stack student platform using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. My main task was to help build the student dashboard, where users could view their assignments, deadlines, and basic profile information.

We had to choose between two approaches for displaying the student data. One option was to load everything at once when the page opened, and the other was to load only the information the user needed as they moved through the site. At first, loading everything seemed simpler because it would be easier to build and test. But after discussing it with my team, we realized it could make the page slower and less organized as the project grew.

I was responsible for the dashboard section, so I focused on making the page feel responsive and easy to use. We decided to go with the second approach and load the data in smaller parts. That meant a little more planning on our side, but it made the site cleaner and easier to maintain.

From that project, I learned that the simplest option is not always the best one. I also got better at thinking about the user experience, not just the code.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database system in Python that exposed a REST API for creating, reading, and updating records. We started seeing inconsistent behavior where some requests were returning 500 errors, and in a few cases data wasn’t being saved correctly. I took ownership of debugging it because I was the one most familiar with the API layer and the logging setup.

I started by reproducing the issue with Postman and then traced the request flow through the API handlers, service layer, and database calls. I added more structured logs around the request ID, payload, SQL query, and exception handling so I could see exactly where the failure happened. That helped me find two main problems: one endpoint was not validating a required field before writing to the database, and another query was using the wrong parameter order, which caused records to be inserted with mismatched values.

I fixed the validation logic, corrected the query parameters, and added clearer error responses so the API would return a 400 for bad input instead of failing silently. I also updated the logs so each request had enough context to debug faster in the future.

After the changes, the 500 errors dropped to zero in our test runs, and the API became much more reliable. We were able to complete the project with stable create and update operations, and I also cut debugging time significantly because the logs made issues much easier to trace.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python REST API for managing student assignments, and I personally owned the debugging when one endpoint started returning inconsistent results in production-like testing. The issue was with the `GET /assignments/{id}` endpoint: sometimes it returned a 500 error, and other times it returned incomplete data even though the record existed in the database.

I started by checking the application logs and comparing successful and failing requests. I noticed the failures were happening only when the assignment had no related submission record yet. The API was trying to access `submission.status` directly, but for new assignments that relationship was `None`, so it was throwing an `AttributeError`. I reproduced it locally with a test case, then traced the request flow through the controller, service layer, and database query to confirm the root cause.

I fixed it by adding a null check in the service layer and updating the response mapping so the API would return a default value like `"not_submitted"` instead of crashing. I also added two unit tests: one for an assignment with a submission and one without. After that, the endpoint stopped failing, and the error rate for that route dropped from about 15% in my test runs to 0%. It also made the response more consistent, which helped the frontend handle the data correctly.

One project I worked on was a React web app that used Firebase for the backend. It was a course project, so the goal was to build something practical while learning how to put the pieces together. The app let users sign up, log in, and manage some basic information in a simple interface.

My role was mostly to assist with the frontend work. I helped build a few of the pages in React, connected parts of the UI to Firebase, and fixed bugs when things weren’t working as expected. I also worked with the rest of the team to make sure the app stayed organized and that the main features were easy to use.

It was a good experience for me because I got more comfortable working with React and learned how a web app can be connected to a backend service like Firebase. In the end, we had a working project that met the basic requirements and gave me a better understanding of how to build and troubleshoot a real application.

I also got some experience figuring out how to structure components and make the app feel more consistent. It was a good learning experience for me because I got to practice working with React in a more real project setting instead of just doing small exercises.

Overall, the project went well and helped me get more comfortable with JavaScript and React, especially with how a web app comes together from start to finish.

question: Tell me about a software project you worked on.
answer:
One project I worked on was a React web app I built as part of my course work. It was a simple portfolio-style application where users could view different sections of content, like an about page, project cards, and a contact area.

My main responsibility was building the front end and making sure the page looked clean and worked smoothly. I used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and React to create the layout and handle the different components. I also worked on making the design responsive so it would still look good on smaller screens.

One challenge I ran into was keeping the components organized as the app started to grow. At first, I had some repeated code, so I spent time breaking things into smaller reusable pieces. That made the project easier to manage and helped me understand React better.

Overall, it was a really good learning experience for me because it helped me practice building a real web app from start to finish, and it gave me more confidence working with React and front-end development in general.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I delivered a reporting feature under a pretty tight constraint: we needed to add a new analytics summary endpoint without changing the existing API contract, because another part of the app was already depending on it. I personally owned the work from design through implementation and testing.

The feature was for an analytics reporting tool built with Node.js and REST APIs. The requirement was to return a compact report with totals, date-based breakdowns, and a few key metrics, but I had to keep the response shape backward compatible and avoid adding any heavy database work that would slow the endpoint down. So I started by reviewing the existing route structure and the current test coverage to understand what I could safely extend.

I broke the work into small pieces. First, I added a new service layer function to gather the raw data and calculate the summary values in Node.js instead of putting too much logic directly in the route handler. Then I updated the REST endpoint to call that service and return the report in the same general format as the existing API. Because performance was a concern, I kept the queries focused and avoided extra round trips by reusing data where possible and shaping the response in one place.

Testing was a big part of the constraint, because I wanted to make sure I didn’t break the existing behavior. I wrote unit tests for the calculation logic, especially around edge cases like empty datasets, zero values, and date boundaries. I also added API tests to verify the response status, payload structure, and that the old fields still came back exactly as expected. When a couple of tests failed at first, it helped me catch a mismatch in how I was formatting dates, so I fixed that before merging.

What I learned from it was how important it is to work within existing boundaries and still keep the code clean. I had to be careful about backward compatibility, test coverage, and keeping the implementation simple enough to maintain.

question: Tell me about a time you improved an application or system.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a small database management system built with Python and a REST API. I was responsible for debugging one of the core flows where records were being saved correctly, but sometimes the API would return inconsistent results when users queried them right after an update.

I started by tracing the issue through the request logs and application logs, then reproduced it locally with a few test cases. I found that the problem was caused by a mismatch between when the database transaction was committed and when the API response was being generated. In some cases, the code was reading from a stale in-memory object instead of re-fetching the updated record from the database.

I fixed it by changing the update endpoint to commit first, then query the database again before returning the response. I also added more structured logging around the request lifecycle so I could see the record ID, operation type, and transaction status in the logs. After that, I wrote a few additional tests for update-and-read behavior to make sure the API returned the latest data consistently.

As a result, the inconsistent responses stopped, and the failing test cases went from intermittent to passing reliably. It also made debugging much easier because the logs clearly showed where each request was in the flow.

question: Describe a project where you had to choose between two technical approaches.
answer:
In my student platform project, I had to choose between building the front end as one single page with sections that showed and hid content, or creating separate pages for each part of the site. The platform was for students to view course information, assignments, and announcements, and I was responsible for the front-end structure and interaction using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

At first, I thought a single-page approach would be simpler because it would feel smoother for users and I could keep everything in one place. But after planning it out, I realized that separate pages would be easier to organize, especially since the project had different sections with different content. It also made it easier for me to keep the code cleaner and update each part without affecting the others.

I chose the separate-page approach, and that worked well for the project. It made navigation clearer, and it was easier for me to test and fix issues as I built it. The main thing I learned was that the “best” technical choice depends on the size of the project and how much structure it needs, not just what seems easiest at the start.

question: Tell me about a feature you delivered under a constraint.
answer:
On my portfolio project, I worked on an analytics reporting tool, and I was responsible for delivering a new reporting endpoint under a pretty tight constraint: we had to add the feature without breaking the existing REST API contract, and I had a limited amount of time to get it done.

The feature was a summary report that pulled usage data and returned it in a format the frontend could consume quickly. I owned the implementation end to end in Node.js, so I started by checking the current API structure and the existing test coverage to make sure I understood what I could safely change. The main constraint was that the data model wasn’t ideal for reporting, so instead of redesigning everything, I built the endpoint to work with the current shape of the data and did the aggregation in the service layer.

I split the work into a few steps. First, I added the REST route and controller. Then I wrote the service logic to calculate the metrics, like totals and grouped counts, from the raw records. I kept the logic small and testable so I could verify each part separately. After that, I added tests for the happy path, empty data, and a few edge cases like missing fields and invalid query parameters. I used the tests to protect the existing behavior, because I didn’t want the new report to affect the other endpoints.

One thing I had to be careful about was performance. Since the report could involve a larger dataset, I avoided doing unnecessary work in the controller and kept the response payload focused on only the fields the frontend needed. I also made sure the API returned consistent status codes and error messages so it would be easy to integrate.

That experience taught me how to deliver something useful even when the ideal solution isn’t possible. I had to stay within the existing API design, keep the code clean, and rely on tests to make sure the feature was safe to ship.

question: Describe a technical problem you solved in a project.
answer:
In a course project, I worked on a Python backend REST API for managing student course data, and I ran into a bug where one endpoint was intermittently returning 500 errors in production-like testing. I personally owned the debugging because I had written that part of the API.

I started by checking the server logs and noticed the failures only happened when the request payload was missing an optional field. The traceback pointed to a `KeyError` in the request parsing logic, where I was accessing `data["course_id"]` directly instead of using a safer validation step. I also found that the error handling was too generic, so the API was hiding the real issue behind a 500 instead of returning a clear 400 response.

I fixed it by adding explicit input validation before the business logic ran, using `data.get()` where appropriate, and returning structured JSON error messages with the correct HTTP status codes. I also added log messages around the request body and validation failures so future debugging would be easier.

After the fix, the endpoint stopped crashing, and the error rate for that route went from several failures during testing to zero in the final test run. It also made the API behavior clearer, because invalid requests now return a proper 400 response instead of failing unexpectedly.

question: Tell me about something you learned during your studies.
answer:
One thing I learned during my studies was how much my understanding improves when I don’t just try to memorize the material, but actually talk it through with other people. In one of my coursework classes, we had to work through a topic that seemed pretty straightforward at first, but once we started discussing it as a group, I realized I had only understood part of it.

I wasn’t the most confident at first, so I mostly listened and tried to follow along, but I did contribute when I could and asked questions when something didn’t make sense. That helped me see that it’s okay not to understand everything immediately. I also learned that different people approach the same assignment in very different ways, and that can make the whole process better.

Overall, it made me more comfortable with group work and more aware that learning is not just about getting the right answer, but also about building understanding step by step.
